## 1 | INTRODUCTION

Condensed fuel emulation began in the 1960s. Initial studies using gaseous fuels to emulate pool fires were performed by Corlett. 1-3 De Ris and Orloff 4,5 performed separate research. These studies proved that condensed fuel flames could be emulated. More recently, Quintiere and co-workers 6-11 have developed improved burners and procedures including a calorimeter for more reliable net heat flux measurement.

metadata.source: Emulation of condensed fuel flames with gaseous fuels supplied through a porous copper calorimeter (1)

text: It is possible to emulate the burning characteristics of solid and liquid fuels using a gaseous fuel/inert mixture. This was recently performed for four condensed fuels using a burner called the burning rate emulator (BRE). 6,7 The emulation involves matching four key fuel properties: heat of combustion, laminar smoke point, heat of gasification, and surface temperature (Δhc, LSP, L, and Ts). 6 Matching the heat of gasification requires determining the heat flux to the burner surface.

metadata.source: Emulation of condensed fuel flames with gaseous fuels supplied through a porous copper calorimeter (1)

text:
The first BRE burner, BRE 1, was used in normal gravity and microgravity. 6,7 The second burner, BRE 2, was used for ignition and extinction studies 8,10 and in drop-tower tests. 9 These studies measured the burner heat flux with embedded heat flux sensors. ## Summary

metadata.source: Emulation of condensed fuel flames with gaseous fuels supplied through a porous copper calorimeter (1)

text: The burning rate emulator (BRE) is a burner that emulates condensed fuel flames using gaseous fuel/inert mixtures by matching four properties: the heat of combustion; the heat of gasification; the laminar smoke point; and the surface temperature. Matching the heat of gasification requires measuring the burner heat flux, for which the BRE has embedded heat flux gauges and a copper top-plate calorimeter. Seven condensed fuels were emulated: acetone, ethanol, methanol, polyethylene, polymethylmethacrylate, polypropylene, and polystyrene

metadata.source: Emulation of condensed fuel flames with gaseous fuels supplied through a porous copper calorimeter (1)

text: . The gaseous fuels were methane, ethylene, and propylene, diluted with nitrogen. Emulation data and flame images are shown to demonstrate emulation accuracy. A new method of emulation is developed that shifts the focus on which properties are prioritized and yields ~15% improvement in flame height. Calibration and use of the calorimeter are shown to have improved accuracy (within 5%) which provides confidence in the results.

Thus motivated, this study uses the BRE 2 burner enabled with a slug calorimeter to emulate the burning of several condensed fuels. ## 2 | EXPERIMENTAL

metadata.source: Emulation of condensed fuel flames with gaseous fuels supplied through a porous copper calorimeter (1)

text:
## 2 | EXPERIMENTAL

The BRE 2 has a stainless-steel base plate and sidewalls, a ceramic flow-straightener, two embedded Medtherm Schmidt-Boelter type heat flux gauges, and a 7-mm thick porous copper top plate that serves as the burner surface. 9 Heat flux sensors are located at values of R = 0 mm (center) and R * (offset), and the surface includes two K-type thermocouples embedded in the underside of the copper plate. 9 A schematic of the 50 mm diameter BRE 2 burner is provided in Figure 1. 9 For this study, a 25 mm version of this burner was used, with R * = 8.25 mm.

metadata.source: Emulation of condensed fuel flames with gaseous fuels supplied through a porous copper calorimeter (1)

text: Uniformly painting the burner and sensors with the same paint ensures that these surfaces have the same absorptivity (α) and emissivity (ϵ). Rustoleum high heat paint has measured absorptivity and emissivity values in excess of 0.91 and was shown to be more thermally durable than other high emissivity paints. 17 Having uniformity of these surface properties simplifies the heat transfer between the sensor and burner surfaces, which is helpful for accurate calibration and flame heat transfer. 6 The 25 mm BRE 2 burner with a fresh coat of Rustolem paint is shown in Figure 2.

## 2.2 | Calorimeter calibration

As previously mentioned, the burner surface can be used as a calorimeter for an additional determination of net heat flux across the surface. It must be calibrated, during which a radiation shield prevents the back of the burner from being directly heated by the propane heater. 19 Like the heat sensor calibration, the heat flux is varied in steps to determine calibration constants. Five 90 seconds steps were performed to test the calorimeter's effectiveness for up to 500 seconds.

## 2.3 | Emulation of condensed fuels

text: The present burner contains a calorimeter that can be used to determine the net heat flux to the entire burner surface. This improves the accuracy in measuring heat flux and heat of gasification. The calorimeter also responds more quickly. text: The described method of flame emulation is not ideal for all condensed fuels. Due to their relatively low smoke point (compared to gaseous fuels), some sooty condensed fuel flames, such as aromatics, may be difficult to emulate. Furthermore, charring materials may also be poor candidates for flame emulation because they do not typically achieve steady burning.

[Figure] 
This figure presents a series of photographs comparing the flame characteristics of four condensed polymer fuels (PP, HDPE, PS, PMMA) with gaseous fuels (C3H6/N2, C2H4/N2) supplied through a porous copper calorimeter. The images are arranged in pairs for each polymer, showing the flame height and shape relative to a specific gaseous fuel.

1.  **Figure Content:** The figure displays eight vertical flame images. Each polymer (PP, HDPE, PS, PMMA) is paired with a gaseous fuel. Yellow scale bars indicate the approximate flame height.
2.  **Experimental Conditions:** The setup involves a porous copper calorimeter. The gaseous fuels are mixtures of hydrocarbons and nitrogen (C3H6/N2, C2H4/N2). The condensed fuels are Polypropylene (PP), High-Density Polyethylene (HDPE), Polystyrene (PS), and Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA).
3.  **Readable Values:**
    *   **PP:** Flame height approx. 50 mm (scale bar).
    *   **C3H6/N2:** Flame height approx. 50 mm (scale bar).
    *   **HDPE:** Flame height approx. 50 mm (scale bar).
    *   **PS:** Flame height approx. 100 mm (scale bar).
    *   **C3H6/N2 (paired with PS):** Flame height approx. 100 mm (scale bar).
    *   **PMMA:** Flame height approx. 100 mm (scale bar).
    *   **C2H4/N2:** Flame height approx. 100 mm (scale bar).
4.  **Observed Behavior:** The gaseous flames (C3H6/N2, C2H4/N2) exhibit a distinct blue base (premixed zone) transitioning to a yellow/orange tip (diffusion zone). The condensed fuel flames (PP, HDPE, PS, PMMA) appear predominantly yellow/orange, indicating diffusion-limited combustion. The flame heights for the gaseous fuels are matched to the condensed fuels in the pairs (e.g., the C3H6/N2 flame is scaled to match the PP and PS flames). The PS and PMMA flames are visibly taller (approx. 100 mm) compared to the PP and HDPE flames (approx. 50 mm).
5.  **Fire-Safety Implication:** The figure demonstrates that gaseous fuels can be tuned to emulate the flame height and heat release characteristics of specific condensed polymer fuels, which is useful for fire safety testing and modeling.

text:
[Figure] FIGURE 6 Emulation of liquid fuels using flow-matching method
Figure 6 presents a visual comparison of flame shapes and sizes to demonstrate the "emulation of liquid fuels using flow-matching method." The figure consists of six panels arranged in three pairs, each comparing a condensed fuel (liquid) flame with a gaseous fuel flame supplied through a porous copper calorimeter.

1.  **Panel 1 (Left):**
    *   **Methanol:** A liquid fuel flame with a pinkish-orange upper body and a blue base. A yellow scale bar indicates a height of **100 mm**.
    *   **CH4/N2:** A gaseous fuel flame (Methane/Nitrogen mixture) with a blue base and a yellow-orange upper body. It is visually similar in height to the methanol flame.

2.  **Panel 2 (Center):**
    *   **Ethanol:** A liquid fuel flame with a bright white/yellow body and a blue base. A yellow scale bar indicates a height of **150 mm**.
    *   **C2H4/N2:** A gaseous fuel flame (Ethylene/Nitrogen mixture) with a bright white/yellow body and a blue base. It is visually similar in height to the ethanol flame.

3.  **Panel 3 (Right):**
    *   **Acetone:** A liquid fuel flame with a bright white/yellow body and a blue base. A yellow scale bar indicates a height of **150 mm**.
    *   **C2H4/N2:** A gaseous fuel flame (Ethylene/Nitrogen mixture) with a bright white/yellow body and a blue base. It is visually similar in height to the acetone flame.

**Experimental Conditions:**
*   **Gravity:** Not stated (likely normal gravity based on flame shape, though the paper context is microgravity emulation).
*   **Fuel:** Methanol, Ethanol, Acetone (liquids); CH4/N2, C2H4/N2 (gases).
*   **Apparatus:** Porous copper calorimeter (implied by caption and context).

**Observed Behavior:**
The figure demonstrates that gaseous fuels (CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2) can be tuned to produce flames that match the size and shape of specific liquid fuel flames (Methanol, Ethanol, Acetone). The CH4/N2 flame emulates Methanol (approx. 100 mm), while the C2H4/N2 flame emulates both Ethanol and Acetone (approx. 150 mm). The flames exhibit typical diffusion flame characteristics with blue bases (combustion zone) and yellow/white upper regions (soot incandescence).

**Fire-Safety Implication:**
This method allows researchers to study the combustion characteristics of hazardous or difficult-to-handle liquid fuels using safer, controllable gaseous surrogates that replicate the flame's thermal and visual properties.

## 3 | RESULTS

In the first method, for each condensed fuel, a gaseous mixture with the same heat of combustion and a similar smoke point was burned at the same mass flux. In most cases, the heat of gasification and flame height were nearly the same. For example, as detailed in Table 2, the ethylene/nitrogen mixture nearly matched the known heat of gasification for ethanol. 23 This process was followed for each condensed fuel, as shown in Table 2.

text: Images of the condensed fuels adjacent to their emulations are shown in Figures 5 and 6 for solids and liquids. Images show close agreement of color and shape between condensed and emulated flames. While not perfect, the emulated flame heights are on average within ±27% of the measured condensed fuel flame heights. The clear visual resemblance demonstrates the ability to emulate condensed fuels.

text: Some discrepancies exist between the condensed and gaseous fuels with regards to both heat of gasification and appearance. These may be due to an imperfect measurement of the steady mass loss rate of each condensed fuel. This may be partially explained by the uncertainties present in the condensed fuel burning apparatus. PP and HDPE were difficult to ignite and probably did not attain steady burning, which may have resulted in an inaccurate heat of gasification value.

text: A second method was employed to more closely match fuel properties. In this method, the gaseous fuel mass flux was adjusted to match the heat of gasification of the condensed fuel (instead of matching its mass flux). This was performed for all fuels except ethanol, acetone, and PS, whose heats of gasification were already matched with the first method. The results are shown in Figure 7 and summarized in Table 3.

metadata.source: Emulation of condensed fuel flames with gaseous fuels supplied through a porous copper calorimeter (1)

text:
For methanol and PMMA, this method required only a 20% decrease in flow but improved the emulation in terms of flame appearance and emulation properties (flame height within +10%). To match L for PP and HDPE, mass fluxes more than twice those of the condensed fuels were required. Consequently, the emulated flames are too tall. This behavior arises because these condensed fuels did not attain steady burning, which prevented them from reaching their true steady burning flame height. This indicates steady burning is imperative for emulation of condensed fuel flames.

## 4 | CONCLUSIONS

metadata.source: Emulation of condensed fuel flames with gaseous fuels supplied through a porous copper calorimeter (1)

text:
## 4 | CONCLUSIONS

Seven condensed fuels were burned and emulated with gaseous fuels. The principal conclusions are as follows.

Condensed fuels can be roughly emulated with gases when the heat of combustion, laminar smoke point, and fuel mass flux are matched (method 1). For the eight emulations performed here, the flame lengths agree, on average, within ±27%. The emulations are especially successful for ethanol, acetone, and PS, whose heats of gasification happened to be matched with the gaseous fuels.

metadata.source: Emulation of condensed fuel flames with gaseous fuels supplied through a porous copper calorimeter (1)

text: For fuels whose heats of gasification are not matched with method 1, improved emulations are obtained by matching the heat of combustion, laminar smoke point, and heat of gasification (method 2). For fuels that burned steadily (methanol and PMMA), method 2 produced emulation flame heights that were only 10% higher than their respective condensed fuels on average, compared to 27% using method 1.

metadata.source: Emulation of condensed fuel flames with gaseous fuels supplied through a porous copper calorimeter (1)

text:
Because successful emulations require matching heat of gasification, the burner heat flux must be measured. This can be done with heat flux gauges, but a porous copper slug calorimeter can determine the net heat flux more appropriately. The slug calorimeter was found to be accurate (and to agree within 5%).

Some condensed fuels, particularly solids, are difficult to ignite and slow to reach steady burning. Successful emulations require steady condensed fuel flames.
